title: Building Four Optimizers Racing Down the Same Hill
concept_layer: gradient descent: θ(t+1) = θ(t) - η∇f(θ); learning as descending a landscape; optimizer variants as different descent strategies
technique_first: partial derivative approximation via finite differences
domain_deferred: second-order methods (Newton, natural gradient) → later ML maps
non-differentiable optimization → swarm (already covered) + genetic (already covered)

capture_leaks.two_dimensional_loss: We visualize 2D loss (θ₁, θ₂) as a 3D surface. Real ML has millions of dimensions; intuition from 2D is partial — saddle points dominate high-D.
capture_leaks.smooth_differentiable_surface: The surfaces here are nice polynomials. Real loss landscapes have cliffs, plateaus, discontinuities — which is why modern optimizers use clipping, warmup, schedules.
capture_leaks.fixed_loss_function: Each run optimizes a static function. Real ML has STOCHASTIC loss (mini-batches give noisy gradients). The artifact hints at this but doesn't demonstrate it.
capture_leaks.no_regularization: We descend pure loss. Real training adds regularization (L2, dropout) whose effect on the landscape is profound. Deferred.
capture_leaks.single_basin_thinking: Players will see optimizers converge to A minimum and think 'solved.' In practice, most losses have many comparable minima and WHICH one you reach matters. Mode connectivity is deep — deferred.

limit: Four colored particles race down a hill. They all reach the bottom eventually. But they take different routes, different times, different directions — and those differences are the history of 70 years of numerical optimization. What the artifact refuses: high-dimensional reality, stochasticity, regularization, the politics of loss functions. Each is a door. This is where the 'optimization' word becomes tangible.

grammar_alignment.note: gradient_descent_visualization teaches optimize_gradient — the core atom of modern ML. Classification is gradient descent with a specific loss. Evolution is gradient-free variant. Generation is gradient descent on a generative model. All ML operations compose from this one — plus the specific loss you choose.

biome_alignment.note: The 'adaptive' catalyst turns static forms into forms that optimize themselves toward a fitness. Creatures in the biome now learn from encounters — repeated interactions improve their behavior. This is the sequence where the world gets smart.

stages.title: From flock to gradient
stages.thinking: SwarmIntelligence_Boids taught that coordination is geometry — many agents with local rules yielding collective behavior. Now one agent, no neighbors, but with a 'local rule' of a different kind: follow the slope. If you can feel which direction goes DOWN, you can reach the bottom. That’s it. Optimization. No neighbors, no fitness evaluation over a population — just the local derivative and the step.
stages.code:
# Boids: many agents, local neighbor rules → collective flock
# Gradient descent: ONE agent, local slope rule → finds valleys
#
# Rule: go downhill.
# What you know locally: the gradient (slope vector).
# What you don't know: the global shape of the landscape.
#
# θ(t+1) = θ(t) - η · ∇f(θ)
#   θ    parameters (position on landscape)
#   f(θ) loss function (elevation)
#   ∇f    gradient (direction of steepest ascent)
#   η    learning rate (step size)
#
# This equation trained every neural network you've used.

stages.title: The loss surface — terrain you cannot fully see
stages.thinking: We need something to descend. A loss function: f(θ₁, θ₂). Build a 3D surface where height = f(x, y). For this artifact, multiple test surfaces cycle: a bowl (easy), a saddle (hard), a nonlinear bumpy landscape, Rosenbrock’s banana valley (classic). The player sees the surface from above AND walks on it. Colors encode height. The surface IS the problem.
stages.code:
enum Surface { BOWL, SADDLE, ROSENBROCK, HIMMELBLAU }

func _compute_loss(x: float, y: float, surface: int) -> float:
	match surface:
		Surface.BOWL:
			return x * x + y * y
		Surface.SADDLE:
			return x * x - y * y
		Surface.ROSENBROCK:
			var a = 1.0 - x
			var b = y - x * x
			return a * a + 100.0 * b * b
		Surface.HIMMELBLAU:
			var u = x * x + y - 11.0
			var v = x + y * y - 7.0
			return u * u + v * v
	_:
		return 0.0

# Each function teaches a different lesson:
#   BOWL → convex, one minimum, easy
#   SADDLE → saddle point, SGD gets stuck
#   ROSENBROCK → narrow curved valley
#   HIMMELBLAU → four minima, which do you reach?

stages.title: Compute the gradient — finite differences
stages.thinking: The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives. We could compute it analytically (since we know the surface formula) but for generality we use finite differences: evaluate the surface at (x+h, y) and (x-h, y), subtract, divide by 2h. This gives the partial with respect to x. Do the same for y. The gradient points in the direction of steepest ASCENT. We go in the OPPOSITE direction — downhill.

stages.title: Vanilla SGD — the simplest optimizer
stages.thinking: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) in its simplest form: compute the gradient, step against it, scaled by learning rate. That’s the whole algorithm. Works great on the bowl. Slow in narrow valleys (Rosenbrock). Gets stuck at saddle points. But it’s the baseline. Every optimizer variant is 'SGD plus a trick to fix some specific failure mode.'
stages.code:
class SGD:
	var position: Vector2
	var learning_rate: float = 0.01
	
	func step(grad: Vector2) -> void:
		position -= grad * learning_rate

# θ(t+1) = θ(t) - η · ∇f(θ)
# No memory. No adaptation. Just: here's the slope, step against it.
#
# SGD failures the other optimizers fix:
#   - slow in long narrow valleys   → Momentum
#   - overshoots at bottom           → Nesterov
#   - different scales per parameter → Adam

stages.title: Momentum — accumulate velocity
stages.thinking: SGD forgets where it was going. Momentum remembers: velocity accumulates between steps. Like a ball rolling downhill, it gains speed in consistent directions and resists direction changes. In narrow valleys (like Rosenbrock’s banana), momentum lets the optimizer COAST along the bottom instead of zigzagging between walls. The price: it can overshoot the minimum, which is why the next optimizer (Nesterov) adds a lookahead correction.
stages.code:
class Momentum:
	var position: Vector2
	var velocity: Vector2 = Vector2.ZERO
	var learning_rate: float = 0.01
	var beta: float = 0.9  # momentum coefficient
	
	func step(grad: Vector2) -> void:
		velocity = velocity * beta - grad * learning_rate
		position += velocity

# velocity is the exponentially-decayed average of past gradients
#   beta = 0.0  → same as SGD
#   beta = 0.9  → strong memory of past direction
#   beta = 0.99 → can oscillate, overshoot
#
# 'Heavy ball' metaphor: accumulated momentum pushes through saddles.

stages.title: Nesterov — lookahead momentum
stages.thinking: Momentum pushes you forward, but you only compute the gradient AT your current position. Nesterov’s trick: compute the gradient at the position you’re ABOUT to reach given your momentum. This is a lookahead. If the momentum is carrying you into an upslope, Nesterov notices earlier and corrects earlier. Convergence is faster on curved paths. It’s the same algorithm as Momentum with one line changed — and that one line gave Nesterov his name.
stages.code:
class Nesterov:
	var position: Vector2
	var velocity: Vector2 = Vector2.ZERO
	var learning_rate: float = 0.01
	var beta: float = 0.9
	
	func step_nesterov(f_callable: Callable) -> void:
		# Look ahead: where will we be after momentum?
		var lookahead_pos = position + velocity * beta
		# Compute gradient AT the lookahead position
		var grad = f_callable.call(lookahead_pos)
		# Now update as momentum
		velocity = velocity * beta - grad * learning_rate
		position += velocity

# The lookahead lets you 'see' your future position
# before committing. One line of difference. Massive improvement.

stages.title: Adam — adapt learning rate per parameter
stages.thinking: Adam combines momentum (first moment) with per-parameter learning rates (second moment). It scales each update by the inverse square root of an exponentially-averaged squared-gradient. Parameters with large recent gradients get SMALLER updates; parameters with small gradients get LARGER updates. Adaptive. Robust. The default optimizer for most of deep learning since 2015. In the race, it usually wins.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: Four racers on one hill. All obey the local-gradient rule. None can see the full landscape. SGD is honest and slow. Momentum is energetic but impulsive. Nesterov is careful. Adam is smart. In 30 seconds of visualization, the player sees why the 2010s were Adam’s decade. The critical parameter is learning_rate because it sits between two failure modes: too small, endless creep; too large, wild oscillation. That balance is the whole game.
